questions.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ with vertices $(-1,-1),(1,-1),(1,2),$ and $(-1,2),$ traversed counterclockwise. Using the flux form of Green's theorem, express the flux of the vector field
$F(x,y)=(6xy+y{x}^{2})\,i-{y}^{2}\,j$
through $C$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14235132/assets/861b873005c03ea6c25255f2febc975ff153d939780ec46e4f4503cbb50640dc.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=6xy+y{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=-{y}^{2}.$ So,  

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=6y+2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 2\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(6y+2xy)+(-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{2}2y(2+x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{2y}+4x,\,{x}^{7}-{y}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the square $-1\le x\le 0,-1\le y\le 0.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14235132/assets/09acd3df62b333bdaeb7553599507d4dbad7412ef2770b00e8fc8855b38a774e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{2y}+4x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{7}-{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=4,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le 0,\,-1\le y\le 0\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)[x]_{-1}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\cdot 1\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4-2y)\,dy \\  & =[4y-{y}^{2}]_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(4(-1)-(-1)^{2}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨x+\sqrt{y},\,y+\sqrt{x}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and the line $y=0$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14235132/assets/e570374b37c116e32c3a7762b8cf09a28bdbb3e06b5e67e25837902a89bcd264.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x+\sqrt{y}$ and $Q(x,y)=y+\sqrt{x}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-\frac{\pi }{2}\le x\le \frac{\pi }{2},\,0\le y\le \operatorname{cos}⁡x\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}y\,{|}_{0}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,dx \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(1-(-1)) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨y{e}^{y}-4xy,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-4x{y}^{3}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the rectangle with vertices $(0,-1),(1,-1),(1,1),$ and $(0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14235132/assets/f7400787e09600d370fa5c554e616fad6ba3a126a09725cfb236502f81a7e70e.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y{e}^{y}-4xy$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-4x{y}^{3}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-12x{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the rectangular region $D$ as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4y-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4y-12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-4xy-6{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,{|}_{0}^{1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[(-4(1)^{2}y-6(1)^{2}{y}^{2})-0]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(-4y-6{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & =[-2{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =(-2(1)^{2}-2(1)^{3})-(-2(-1)^{2}-2(-1)^{3}) \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the flux form of Green's theorem to calculate the flux of the vector field

$$
F(x,y)=⟨-x,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}⟩
$$

through the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=-y+1,$ $\,x={e}^{y},$ and the line $y=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $F=P\,i+Q\,j,$ and $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then the flux form of Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∬}_{D}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}A,
$$

which is equivalent to

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14235132/assets/728036ffc90e2476017b3102b6279f9c5900f0e7fc58536e76c9aa038eb04f02.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=-x$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):-y+1\le x\le {e}^{y},\,0\le y\le 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem in flux form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,dy-Q\,dx \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}[x]_{-y+1}^{{e}^{y}}\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}({e}^{y}+y-1)\,dy \\  & =-{[{e}^{y}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-[(e+\frac{1}{2}-1)-1] \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-e.\end{aligned}
$$
